lines: Saturday, 16 May 2026
Housekeeping
PRESIDENT:  This is the third day of the evidentiary hearing
in DIAC case no. 240079 between China State Construction
Engineering Corporation (Middle East) LLC and
Dubai Integrated Economic Zones Authority.
By way of housekeeping -- good morning, do take
a seat -- I imagine that everybody is aware that next
week there are two days of problems on the Underground.
Just so people may need to think about their internal
logistics; I hope it won't affect the hearing.
As we know, Mr Choat will always be exactly on time!
A couple of queries.  One is: I've been trying to
find out -- and I'm sure it's in the quantum joint
statement -- where I find a calculation of liquidated
damages.  The provision seems to be one of those
provisions where you can't decide what the liquidated
damages are until you know whether the variations are
successful.  But I wasn't sure how they split between
the milestones.  I'm sure it's somewhere easily found;
I didn't find it.
The second point is very specifically, Ms Cheng, for
you.  In your opening, coming back to the pleadings,
you referred to the alleged inadmissibility of the
defects counterclaim.  In the way in which you frame it
in your opening submissions, it looks as though you
don't include the media facade as part of the defects
counterclaim.
So just for the avoidance of doubt, do you take the
same point in relation to the media facade as you do in
relation to the drainage and earth pits and all that
sort of thing?
MS CHENG:  Logically, I think the answer should be "yes",
because the same contract clauses apply, but I don't
wish to mislead you at this stage.  So with that
indication, can I come back to you in my closing?
PRESIDENT:  It might not, because you say that your claim
for recovery of the deduction in relation to the media
facade is a valid claim, and therefore it may be that
you have to concede that the merits of the media facade
have to be dealt with, and it might be limited simply to
the claim-over for AED 8 million, I don't know.  I don't
require an answer now; I would just like to know in due
course.
All right.  Do either of my colleagues have
anything?
Apart from those matters, Ms Cheng, any
housekeeping?
MS CHENG:  Yes, sirs.
Again, if I start with things that you have got.
The two new documents adduced with my learned friend's
errata and the one new document for which I was going to
apply, those are agreed, they're in the bundle and
we need not trouble you.
Things you have not got: you will see the glaring
absence of a transcript on your desk.  I'm afraid that
that is, with apologies, coming on Monday.  The print
rooms are shut today.  You also don't have a great stack
of contract documents.  Those again will be with you on
Monday, for the same reason.
But we'd be grateful for confirmation of the format
that each tribunal member would prefer.
PRESIDENT:  Well, transcripts as before.
MS CHENG:  Yes.
PRESIDENT:  So far as I'm concerned, certainly A5,
double-sided.  If it's quite chunky, it might be better
in one of the folders, not spirally bound, because
spirally bound after a while can come apart.  Whatever
is most convenient.
MR THOMAS:  Yes, the same for me.  If it works to have one
small bound file with conditions, particular conditions,
and a separate file of specifications and so on, that's
fine.
MR CHOAT:  And for me, just electronic, and any folders
being put on to the system we have that are equivalent
to the hard copies.
MS CHENG:  Thank you.
PRESIDENT:  That's Mr Thomas and myself being put in our
places!
MS CHENG:  That's exactly what I was thinking!
PRESIDENT:  Mr Rigney, do you have any matters of
housekeeping to raise today?
MR RIGNEY:  Nothing from our side.
PRESIDENT:  Right.  So we have in front of us Mr -- forgive
me if I don't pronounce your name properly --
Subramanian.
MR MOOKKAIAH SUBRAMANIAN (called)
PRESIDENT:  Thank you for coming today.  Are you going to
give your evidence on oath or by affirmation?
WITNESS:  Affirmation.
PRESIDENT:  Could you turn the microphone on.  You should
see a button there.  Yes, that's done it.  Thank you
very much.
Could you repeat after me: I do solemnly ...
WITNESS:  ... I do solemnly ...
PRESIDENT:  ... sincerely and truly ...
WITNESS:  ... sincerely and truly ...
PRESIDENT:  ... declare and affirm ...
WITNESS:  ... declare and affirm ...
PRESIDENT:  ... that the evidence which I shall give ...
WITNESS:  ... that the evidence which I shall give ...
PRESIDENT:  ... shall be the truth ...
WITNESS:  ... shall be truth ...
PRESIDENT:  ... the whole truth ...
WITNESS:  ... the whole truth ...
PRESIDENT:  ... and nothing but the truth.
WITNESS:  ... and nothing but the truth.
PRESIDENT:  Thank you very much.
Yes, Mr Rigney.
MR RIGNEY:  Sir, thank you very much.
Examination-in-chief by MR RIGNEY
MR RIGNEY:  Good morning, Mr Subramanian.
A.  Good morning.
Q.  Could we please have {C11}.  Thank you very much.
Page 1.
Mr Subramanian, if you look at the screen in front
of you, is that the first page of your first witness
statement?
A.  Correct.
Q.  Could we please go to page 60 of the document.  And is
that your name at the bottom of the document,
Mr Subramanian?
A.  Correct.
Q.  And is that the date of 13 June 2025?
A.  Correct.
Q.  And is that your signature?
A.  Yes.
Q.  And is this a witness statement made by you on
A.  Yes.
Q.  Thank you very much.
Please then may we then go to {C12}.  Thank you very
much.
Do you see in front of you, Mr Subramanian, the
first page of your second witness statement?
A.  Correct.
Q.  Please may we go to page 132.  I'm so sorry, is
that ...?  Forgive me.  If we just go to the end of the
main text.  Thank you very much.
Again, do you see there the date of
29 December 2025, Mr Subramanian?
A.  That's right.  I signed it.
Q.  And is that your name?
A.  That is my name.
Q.  And is that your signature above your name?
A.  That is my signature and my name.
Q.  Is this a witness statement made by you on
29 December 2025?
A.  Yes.
Q.  Then, please, could we go to {C15}.  Do you see there
a document entitled "Errata to Mr Subramanian's Witness
Statements", dated 11 May 2026?
A.  Yes.
Q.  Please could we go to page 6, I think, of that document.
There, do you see the date of 11 May 2026?
A.  That is my signature.
Q.  And is that your name and your signature?
A.  Correct.
Q.  Are these errata to your first and second witness
statements which you made on 11 May 2026?
A.  That's right.
Q.  And do your first and second witness statements, taken
together with the errata, represent your full and
complete evidence on the matters which you've been asked
to address?
A.  That's right.
Q.  And taken together, are the facts contained in them true
to the best of your knowledge, information and belief?
A.  Correct.
MR RIGNEY:  Mr Subramanian, thank you very much.  I think
there will be some questions for you.
WITNESS:  Thank you.
Cross-examination by MS CHENG
MS CHENG:  Thank you.  Good morning, Mr Subramanian.  Is it
"Subramanian" or "Subramanian"?
A.  The way you are comfortable.
Q.  I probably will use both, so thank you for that.
Just by way of explanation to you, as you know, both
sides have two barristers.  The way that we've organised
it on this side is that I will be asking you some
questions and then Dr Maciolek, who sits to my right,
will ask you some questions, and there will be a point
at which we hand over.  Just so that you're not
surprised when that happens.
Can I start with some introductory matters.  I think
you've confirmed at the start that the evidence that
you're about to give today will be the truth, the whole
truth, and nothing but the truth.  Do you remember doing
that?
A.  Yes.
Q.  Am I right to say that that is also true of the witness
statements that you've made: they contain the truth,
the whole truth -- the whole truth -- and nothing but
the truth; yes?
A.  Yes, agreed.  Yes.
Q.  And you understand that it's important to give the whole
truth, because if you don't give the entire picture, you
can end up misleading; do you understand that?
A.  I understood.
Q.  Am I right to understand that you reviewed Mr Feng's
first witness statement before you prepared your second
witness statement?
A.  Yes.
Q.  And you prepared your second witness statement to give
the tribunal the whole picture in response to what
Mr Feng has said; is that right?
A.  That's right.
Q.  My third -- I think my last -- introductory point.  Your
first language is Tamil, and I understand that you've
had assistance from those advising DSOA in putting your
statement together and the precise language that you
use, and I make no criticism about that.  But is that
right?
A.  I couldn't get your last point.
Q.  That's because it was an incredibly long and rambling
question.
Am I right to understand that you've had assistance
from the solicitors for DSOA in selecting the precise
language that has gone into your witness statement; yes?
A.  That's right.
Q.  But you've confirmed that the evidence in your statement
is your evidence?
A.  Yes, my evidence.
Q.  And can I take from that that where you didn't
understand the meaning of a word, you asked what it
meant?
A.  Yes, we went through the -- lot of discussions in that
way.
Q.  And you've taken care to ensure that the words you have
used convey exactly what you mean?
A.  That's right.
Q.  Starting at the beginning, and with your role in the
project and with what you can help the tribunal with
today, it's right to say, is it, that you were
responsible for identifying and closing snags and
defects, approving China State's rectification works and
ensuring overall quality control and compliance; yes?
A.  At the end of the projects.
Q.  I'm so sorry.  At the end of the project.
A.  Yes.
Q.  So you were defects only, and your purpose was to find
them and fix them?
A.  I'm not involved during the construction stage.
Quality, I'm not involved.
Q.  So you have no way of knowing the quality of
China State's work as it was going down?
A.  At the construction stage, no.
Q.  No.  And DAR was; yes?  DAR was?  The engineer was
there?
A.  DAR is the main consultant, and they were -- appointed
IBA as an MEP consultant, mechanical, electrical and
plumbing work consultant.
Q.  And DAR also had -- I'm so sorry.  Go ahead.
A.  They are the experts on the MEP systems.
Q.  Correct.  And you would be guided by them?
A.  Yes.
Q.  It's your witness statement that addresses the remedial
works quotations relied on in support of
the counterclaim as well; yes?
A.  Yes.
Q.  So you can help the tribunal with the standard against
which DSOA measured the physical works that are in
the counterclaim after they are completed; yes?
A.  Yes.
Q.  But not the quality of the physical works upon
completion and during construction?
A.  Repeat your question?  I couldn't understand that.
Q.  You can help the tribunal with the standard against
which DSOA measured the quality of China State's work
when they had been submitted for snagging; yes?
A.  Yes.
Q.  But you can't help the tribunal with the quality of
China State's works as they were being constructed and
before they were handed over for snagging?
A.  I still am not very clear of your question.
Q.  Okay.
You have highlighted, as I understand it, in your
witness statements all of the defects on site that are
causing you and your FM team practical problems or
reputational damage; is that right?
A.  That's right.
Q.  And you've painted that whole picture of all of the
defects that are causing you major concern?
A.  Yes.
Q.  You were also responsible, as I understand it, for
signing off China State's testing and commissioning
operations; is that right?
A.  No, I am not signing the document as such.  I am not
signing the document.
Q.  Okay.
A.  I am only giving my comments, because in our structure
it's like that.  Until the completion of the project,
project construction team -- construction team is taking
the lead role.  It's been -- there is a construction
engineer, and which is assisted by IBA, and I were -- on
that period, maybe we are -- I am like an advisory role.
And our team -- because the construction team had
limited-strength manpower, and we had an operation team
and enough manpower, so we have done the physical works
and come back with the comments, and we have given our
comments to construction team, and the construction team
will be coordinating with the consultant and to raise to
the contract.
Q.  Mm-hm.  But in terms of the testing and commissioning
works, you were in charge of the team that inspected
that?
A.  Yes, I am in charge of the team who witnessed.
Q.  I'm so sorry, that's the word that we're looking for.
Thank you.
A.  Yes, who witnessed.
Q.  You're in charge of the team witnessing the testing and
commissioning?
A.  Yes.  And our findings and other -- our findings on
those things, whatever the findings, we are immediately
communicating to construction team, and construction
team is communicating to the consultant.
Q.  So you can help the tribunal with the standard against
which DSOA held China State for the testing,
commissioning and completion of what we call
milestone B; yes?
A.  Yes.
Q.  I want to start, as you do in your witness statement,
with on site and snagging.
So it's right to say that usually snagging is done
by a joint inspection, and what happens is the
contractor explains to the employer and the engineer,
they go to site, they look at the defect.  The
contractor might say, "This is not my scope", "That was
damaged by other people", "This is in fact in
specification tolerances"; yes?  That's what normally
happens?
A.  That is the normal process, but we done the defects(?)
for some time.  And due to the volume of the project and
the multiple disagreements involved, each team was --
again, there will be a contractor in coordination
with -- the contractor will be coordinated and our team
will be visiting.
Q.  Mm-hm.  But there isn't the joint walk?
A.  Joint, yes.
Q.  There isn't the joint walk between the contractor and
the client that normally happens?
A.  Contractor, consultant and the client.
Q.  But in terms of the OnSite process, that was unilateral:
there was one person.  Is that right?
A.  No, it's not one person.
Q.  No, the OnSite -- I'm so sorry.
A.  OnSite application.
Q.  Correct.  Let's call it the --
A.  Yes, OnSite application.  It's an application.
Because of the -- due to the large volume of the
project, normally what we'll do, in the small buildings,
we'll go and make the snags and take a photo, prepare
an Excel statement and post to the contractor, and they
will rectify and finish it off.  It's a normal project.
But considering these 19 buildings -- or alternative
building; I am responsible for 19 buildings over
there -- 19 buildings and multiple disciplines, getting
the -- all the reports and preparing the Excel report,
it's a huge job.  That's why, by the time there was
a software came -- it's called OnSite software -- to
track and close the snags.  This software, we subscribed
for this software and we took it.  It's been there --
the subscription was taken for that software for
the particular time.
Q.  Thank you.  So instead of the on-site system you have
the -- instead of the physical on-site system --
PRESIDENT:  For the benefit of the stenographer, when you're
referring to "OnSite" it's actually a brand name,
OnSite.  So it may help with the transcript in due
course.  Thank you.
MS CHENG:  Thank you.
WITNESS:  We can mention "OnSite app".
MS CHENG:  I think you're right.  That's a good idea.  Let's
proceed on that basis, Mr Subramanian.
So instead of the --
PRESIDENT:  Just to be clear again, so if we have it on
the transcript, it's "OnSite app".  That, I think, is
then something which the stenographer can place
an automatic link to.  I hope that helps.
MS CHENG:  Yes.  Thank you very much.
So you have the OnSite app operating on site.
A.  Yes.
Q.  And you put that in place, or DSOA put that in place,
with the intention of logging each and every snag and
defect in the claimant's works; is that right?
A.  That's right.
Q.  As to who used the OnSite app, DSOA provided the tablet
computers with OnSite installed on them to 10 members of
the facilities management staff and eight members of
DAR's team; is that right?
A.  That's right.
Q.  And of the 10 facilities management tablets, six members
of your staff logged snags; yes?
A.  Correct.
Q.  And that's in addition to the eight DAR team members;
correct?
A.  Yes, there's DAR and then subcontractors, they were
using it.
Q.  So my maths was notoriously bad yesterday, but at least
six and up to 14 different individuals were logging
snags on the same project; that's right?
A.  Yes, but not all are on the same discipline, the same
people what I'm talking about.  Because in the project
there are multiple disciplines.  Like, a civil engineer
is not an expert to raise a snag on mechanical system
and the mechanical engineer is not an expert to raise
a snag on electronic systems.  So that's why we have
a -- discipline-wise, their team was formed, and each
team, that tab was given.
So one person was only civil items; one person,
mechanical items; one person, plumbing items; one
person, electrical; one person, electronic, the fire
alarms and low-current systems; one person is doing the
landscaping and others.  Like that we distribute it, so
one person on team.
That team will have the tab, and they will go and
they will find or get these other snags, and they will
take the photos and develop the project.
Q.  But that said -- can I have {C12-4}, please, just to put
this in a bit of context.  So if I scroll down one page,
please.
A.  Yes, this is --
Q.  This is --
A.  This is the team where I'm --
Q.  This is what you're talking about?
A.  Yes.
Q.  So what we have there is, if we look at "Type of Works",
we've got four people assessing and snagging the MEP
works; is that right?
A.  Yes.
Q.  And item number 6, Mr Gupta is the MEP supervisor, so
he would also have an eye to MEP works, wouldn't he?
A.  Which one?
Q.  Item number 6, Mr Gupta, is the MEP supervisor; yes?
A.  Yes.
Q.  So he would have an eye to -- he would be interested in
and qualified to snag -- the MEP works as well; yes?
A.  Yes.
Q.  I think we agreed that you had told these people to go
on site and find each and every snag; yes?
A.  Yes.
Q.  So even if it was outside of their discipline, if they
saw a snag, they would snag it, wouldn't they?
A.  They done it, by mistaken or not to, it does happen.
But when China State has put this is outside the scope,
that's been taken out and they closed it.  Those -- yes.
Sometimes, in some areas, some fit-out works, here,
as a part of the project, we are also given the fit-out
works at a later stage to China State and the division;
they are also doing it.  When they did the snagging,
some of the fit-out snags also by mistake they add.
So these things are then later clarified in
a meeting and removed those snags.  These are later, to
do with the fit-out, removed, and it is not included in
this project.
Q.  Okay.  But the way that that works chronologically is it
gets entered as a snag first, then China State checks:
is it really a snag, then DSOA agrees that it isn't, but
then it still remains to be closed in the way that
the OnSite app has to be closed; yes?
A.  No, they will put comments: it's outside scope.
Q.  Yes.
A.  Then immediately, once they put "outside scope", the
app, how the system is designed, the person who raised
the snag, he has to close it.
Q.  That's right.
A.  Okay?
Q.  So those are the four steps.
A.  Yes.
Q.  That's --
A.  Not four steps.  The person raising the snag, and it
goes to the contractor.  Contractor is rectified or fix
it.  And then it is going to the consultant, also one
stage verified.  And then it's coming to the final --
the person who raised the complaint closing it.
Q.  That's the process through which you go.
A.  That's it.
Q.  So that's what happens with snags that are outside of
scope.  The same thing happens with snags that are
duplicated; is that right?
A.  The duplications is -- there is no chance.  There is no
chance, because we are -- this application is designed
in such a way that you can define the location, system
and the defects.  So when you -- that means when you
revisit at the same location, you can find it easily.
Q.  But that just tells you where a particular snag is.  If
I have a snag at the top of the wall, I would be
allowed, on the OnSite system, to have a snag at
the bottom of the wall, wouldn't I?  Skirting board?
A.  You know, the most interesting case where it happened,
during the starting stage of the project, when our team
went there to -- first we did, in the apartments,
painting works.  The team went there and they started --
they found the marks there, marks there, marks there.
They took a photo of one snag, take it and put,
"Repainting is required".
What the contractor did, they went, "Oh, this is the
photo you've shown: paint it".  Even though we mentioned
the whole room, they didn't done it.  So when we go for
reinspection, "What is this mark?  What is that mark?"
"Oh, you didn't mention that snag".
Due to this reason, our team also went there and
they started to capture all these snags.
Q.  That's it.  But the system allows you to take a snag at
the top of the wall -- there's a blotch of paint at the
top of the wall, there's missing paint at the bottom,
two different snags; yes?
A.  Correct, yes.
Q.  And that system would allow Mr Gupta to take a picture
of the top of the wall and Mr Nair to take a picture of
the top of the wall and make two snags; yes?
A.  No, no, it's not like that.  Yes, it can be.  But when
we work to -- in order to produce the clashes, we
assigned the discipline to the particular person.  If it
is civil engineering snags, only this person raises it.
So he knows which is raised and which is not raised.
Q.  He knows?
A.  Yes, he knows.
Q.  On-site --
A.  That's how the duplication is avoided.
Q.  That's how you avoid: by just telling people?
A.  Yes.
Q.  I understand.
On-site snagging in both senses, so the people
walking the site and the OnSite app, that seems to me to
be being done by quite junior people.  Am I right about
that?
A.  Yes, that's new peoples, readily experienced peoples.
Q.  But they're quite junior.  So you don't snag, for
example?
A.  "You don't snag" means -- I'm manager, managing the
team, okay?  So 19 buildings, new buildings, plus I have
a portfolio of existing buildings.  So everywhere,
I'm going there, Subramanian cannot take it; correct.
Q.  Yes.
A.  So that's why we call with -- we then -- this team, we
agreed with this team in March and April, around 2008,
you know, even some of them are working for a long time,
and they were already experienced in such a snagging.
Q.  For sure.
A.  So it's not the first time they are doing the snagging.
So we, as a facilities management, these peoples who
are in the field, they have vast experience in their
field.
Q.  Yes, but the senior electricians, the low-current
technicians, they're supervisors.  They're very good at
what they do.
A.  Yes.
Q.  But I think, as you say, they're not managers, they're
not top level; they don't really look at things like the
taking-over certificates, things like that.  They're not
that sort of people, are they?
A.  But they are the people -- if these defects is not
identified properly, they are the people going to suffer
on that.
Q.  Yes, correct.
A.  Yes?  So that is the reason their interest is more than
anybody else, because they want to make sure that that
system is perfectly completed for him to run
the project.
Q.  That's right --
A.  That's right.
Q.  -- because they're the facilities manager.  And if the
paint isn't done perfectly, whose job is it to put
the paint on?
A.  Again, the facilities manager, they come to us and
we will have to bear some cost on that, and the time,
and the customer will ...
Q.  So am I right to understand that the junior guys are on
site, and what they have been told to do is that:
"No defect, whether minor or major ..."
I'm reading from paragraph 15 of your statement,
which happens to be on screen.  You tell the chaps in
the table:
"No defect, whether minor or major, should be
overlooked, particular in a government project of [this]
significance."
Yes?
A.  Yes.  See, defect is defect.  Whether it's major or
minor, defect is a defect: it has to be rectified.
Q.  Yes.  That's what they've got to do: that's their job.
A.  Yes.
Q.  It's got to go down.  And what you do with that
afterwards is not their business, is it?
A.  Once they've worked, when the dispute comes, it will be
escalated to our level.
Q.  Yes.
A.  Because when they put these comments, like the owner of
the dispute -- they are even mentioned in our OnSite
app, if you mention there are disputed snags.  If our
core team is raising the snag and the contractor is
telling it's not his responsibility, he can dispute
the snag on the same app.
So what we did, we usually sit with the contractor
team and we will go through these disputed snags.  Every
period, it would be often, every week we -- every week
or -- it's not exactly every day; it depends on the
value, depends on the availability.  We will sit with
them and we will go through all the disputed snags, and
we agree what should we do and who will be responsible,
and we agree, we closed.
And there are some items which is not -- cannot be
completed amicably: those items, we are taking to
the consultant.
Q.  Yes.
A.  This is the -- because he is the person.  This is the
snag, I am telling, "This is the area to be fixed", they
are telling it is not there, and what is subsequently,
then ask for the consultant this be closed.
So all those disputed snags, it's been completely
closed.  So that's why the disputes are already gone;
there is no level of disputes.
But there are some issues, unclosed snags were
there, like basement water leakages.  Basement water
leakages, we have more than 1,000 snags, only the
basement water leakages.  Those basements, we have water
leakage.  The contractor is telling, "No", this and
that, and he's telling, "Okay, next rain we will see",
all these things.  They make some rectification, "Next
rain, we will see".  The second rain, third rain, even
we are getting the snags.
Q.  Those are disputes; yes?
A.  Yes.  That's why all those items we completely removed
from that and we put in this one, the taking-over
certificate.  These are the issues, not on-site snags
which is not completed at the site related with this
discipline.  Like basement water leakages --
Q.  Yes.
A.  -- the glass damages, and then epoxy coating is one of
the particular issues.  These are all -- mainly all are
civil-related snags which is not completed.
Q.  So if I can summarise that, there's a process of
escalation?
A.  Yes.
Q.  The on-site gentlemen enter the snags on the OnSite app,
they open them, they close them on the OnSite app.
